### How to prepare for the investor questions you will face

**Be ready for: "How do you know you're simpler than Jobber?"**

The analysis placed Tessivane first on both the setup-complexity map and the SMB-native design map. An outside review of this analysis raised a serious concern about both of those rankings: Tessivane's coordinates on each map were set by accepting your own positioning claim — that you are the lowest-complexity option — and then calibrating the number against Jobber and Housecall Pro. No external benchmark independently measures Tessivane's setup experience or SMB-nativeness today.

This is the question investors will ask, and the current answer is circular. Before your next meeting, gather evidence you didn't generate yourself: G2 or Capterra setup scores for Tessivane once you have enough reviews, onboarding completion rates from your paying customers, or a side-by-side setup time comparison run by an independent tester. Even a handful of customer quotes that specifically describe switching from Jobber and why the experience differed is stronger than a self-assigned score. The moment you have a non-self-referential data point, the first-place ranking becomes something you can defend in the room.

**Be ready for: "What's your edge over Jobber and Housecall Pro — aren't they already SMB-focused?"**

Your core differentiation claim — that Tessivane offers lighter-weight UX and pricing designed for smaller service businesses, not enterprise contractors — only partly holds under scrutiny. It is clearly true against ServiceTitan, where verifiable gaps in ease-of-setup scores support the comparison. It weakens significantly against Jobber and Housecall Pro, which already occupy the SMB-friendly field service software position with large installed customer bases.

You will need a sharper answer for this question than "we are simpler." One reframe worth building: Tessivane is built for the 2-to-10 technician shop that finds even Jobber's feature surface to be more than they need right now, and where the owner is still the one doing the scheduling. That is a narrower segment than Jobber addresses, but if it is yours, say so with numbers — how many shops in that range exist, what they currently pay, and why Jobber's pricing and onboarding does not fit them. A segmentation argument is more defensible than a simplicity argument when the incumbents are already in your category.

**Be ready for: "Who else is doing this?" (and know FieldPulse is on their list)**

FieldPulse was surfaced during this analysis's independent research. It targets HVAC, plumbing, and electrical SMBs — the same trades you name — with more than 450 reviews on Capterra, a 4.6 rating, and a direct positioning as field service management for small businesses. An investor who asks about your competitive set is likely to have seen it. Have a clear answer for why Tessivane and FieldPulse are not the same thing, whether that is a feature difference, a segment difference, or a geographic difference — but do not rely on the current analysis to answer that question, because FieldPulse does not appear in it.

### Defensibility roadmap: what to build, in what order

One defensibility dimension is in play today — switching costs — and it is early. Five others have not started yet. Here is how to think about the sequencing.

**Defend and deepen switching costs first.** This is already your strongest dimension (which is a low bar — it is currently weak), but it is also the cheapest to strengthen. The mechanism is workflow depth: the more of a customer's operational history lives inside Tessivane — past jobs, customer notes, recurring schedule patterns, invoice records — the harder it is to leave. Every feature that pulls more of the owner's real workflow into the product adds to this. Target: meaningful job-history depth and customer data portability that makes moving to Jobber feel like starting from scratch.

**Build data advantages in parallel.** As your customer base accumulates job data, you accumulate something competitors without your segment focus cannot easily replicate: a dataset of how 2-to-10-technician shops actually run — seasonal patterns, job type distributions, pricing norms for the trades verticals you serve. That data can improve your product (smarter scheduling suggestions, better invoice templates) and, eventually, become a reason buyers stay. This dimension is already moving in the right direction; the milestone to aim for is a product feature that visibly uses aggregate data to help an individual customer.

**Brand reputation follows customers, not marketing.** With Jobber at 100,000+ customers and Housecall Pro at 2,700+, you are not competing on brand recognition yet. The practical move at this stage is to be findable in the places your buyer looks — trade association forums, HVAC and plumbing subreddits, the Capterra and G2 pages where your competitors are already reviewed — before you have enough reviews to rank. One real customer story from a named contractor in a specific trade is worth more here than a polished case study.

**Network effects and structural cost advantages are not this year's problem.** Field service software does not naturally produce network effects (one HVAC contractor's data does not make the product more valuable for another), and cost structure advantages require scale you have not reached. Do not invest in either dimension now — they are the most expensive moats to build from nothing and offer the least return at the seed stage. The right time to revisit them is when switching costs are moderate and you have a defined data story.

**No patent filings were found in the public record for Tessivane.** If you are describing the product as patent-protected in any investor materials, remove that language — there is no filing to point to. If you have filed and it has not yet published, that will show up in public records within 18 months of filing; until then, say "patent application pending" only if you have a filed application number you can provide on request.

### What you have working in your favor

**Your carved-out position is real.** Across both maps — setup complexity and SMB-native design — no competitor lands ahead of you on both axes at the same time. ServiceTitan dominates platform breadth and scalability, but it is visibly heavier and more enterprise-oriented. Jobber and Housecall Pro are your nearest rivals, but the analysis puts clear space between you and each of them on the dimensions that matter most to your buyer. That is a defensible claim, not a platitude.

**The research on your three established competitors is thorough.** Pricing, funding, team size, and target customers were independently verified for ServiceTitan, Jobber, and Housecall Pro. The analysis does not dismiss their strengths — ServiceTitan's IPO scale, Jobber's 100,000+ customers, and Housecall Pro's AI acceleration are all acknowledged. That intellectual honesty is what makes your competitive framing credible in a diligence conversation.

**Your switching costs are building.** As customers accumulate job history, customer records, and operational workflows inside Tessivane, the cost of moving to another tool rises. That is the one defensibility dimension already in motion, and it is the right one to be building at this stage.

---

### The single highest-leverage fix before your next investor conversation

**Expand and diversify the competitive set.** The analysis covers three companies, all direct competitors. Investors expect to see at least five, and they expect to see more than one category — specifically a do-nothing alternative and at least one emerging entrant alongside the established direct rivals.

The candidates are already identified: FieldPulse (a direct SMB field service tool with nearly all of its reviewers from small businesses in exactly your target trades), the manual-operations alternative (phone calls, paper job cards, and shared spreadsheets — the actual incumbent for most sub-five-technician shops), and at least one of Workiz or Service Fusion as an emerging entrant. Adding these three does not change your position on the existing maps. What it does is show investors that you understand the full consideration set your buyer actually uses — and that you have a clear answer to why someone on spreadsheets would pay for Tessivane rather than continuing to do nothing.

Resolving this also fixes a related gap: right now, all three companies in your landscape are categorized identically, which signals narrow thinking to investors even when the research behind them is strong.

---

### How to prepare for the investor questions you will face

**Be ready for: "How do you know you're simpler than Jobber?"**

The analysis placed Tessivane first on both the setup-complexity map and the SMB-native design map. An outside review of this analysis raised a serious concern about both of those rankings: Tessivane's coordinates on each map were set by accepting your own positioning claim — that you are the lowest-complexity option — and then calibrating the number against Jobber and Housecall Pro. No external benchmark independently measures Tessivane's setup experience or SMB-nativeness today.

This is the question investors will ask, and the current answer is circular. Before your next meeting, gather evidence you didn't generate yourself: G2 or Capterra setup scores for Tessivane once you have enough reviews, onboarding completion rates from your paying customers, or a side-by-side setup time comparison run by an independent tester. Even a handful of customer quotes that specifically describe switching from Jobber and why the experience differed is stronger than a self-assigned score. The moment you have a non-self-referential data point, the first-place ranking becomes something you can defend in the room.

**Be ready for: "What's your edge over Jobber and Housecall Pro — aren't they already SMB-focused?"**

Your core differentiation claim — that Tessivane offers lighter-weight UX and pricing designed for smaller service businesses, not enterprise contractors — only partly holds under scrutiny. It is clearly true against ServiceTitan, where verifiable gaps in ease-of-setup scores support the comparison. It weakens significantly against Jobber and Housecall Pro, which already occupy the SMB-friendly field service software position with large installed customer bases.

You will need a sharper answer for this question than "we are simpler." One reframe worth building: Tessivane is built for the 2-to-10 technician shop that finds even Jobber's feature surface to be more than they need right now, and where the owner is still the one doing the scheduling. That is a narrower segment than Jobber addresses, but if it is yours, say so with numbers — how many shops in that range exist, what they currently pay, and why Jobber's pricing and onboarding does not fit them. A segmentation argument is more defensible than a simplicity argument when the incumbents are already in your category.

**Be ready for: "Who else is doing this?" (and know FieldPulse is on their list)**

FieldPulse was surfaced during this analysis's independent research. It targets HVAC, plumbing, and electrical SMBs — the same trades you name — with more than 450 reviews on Capterra, a 4.6 rating, and a direct positioning as field service management for small businesses. An investor who asks about your competitive set is likely to have seen it. Have a clear answer for why Tessivane and FieldPulse are not the same thing, whether that is a feature difference, a segment difference, or a geographic difference — but do not rely on the current analysis to answer that question, because FieldPulse does not appear in it.

---

### Defensibility roadmap: what to build, in what order

One defensibility dimension is in play today — switching costs — and it is early. Five others have not started yet. Here is how to think about the sequencing.

**Defend and deepen switching costs first.** This is already your strongest dimension (which is a low bar — it is currently weak), but it is also the cheapest to strengthen. The mechanism is workflow depth: the more of a customer's operational history lives inside Tessivane — past jobs, customer notes, recurring schedule patterns, invoice records — the harder it is to leave. Every feature that pulls more of the owner's real workflow into the product adds to this. Target: meaningful job-history depth and customer data portability that makes moving to Jobber feel like starting from scratch.

**Build data advantages in parallel.** As your customer base accumulates job data, you accumulate something competitors without your segment focus cannot easily replicate: a dataset of how 2-to-10-technician shops actually run — seasonal patterns, job type distributions, pricing norms for the trades verticals you serve. That data can improve your product (smarter scheduling suggestions, better invoice templates) and, eventually, become a reason buyers stay. This dimension is already moving in the right direction; the milestone to aim for is a product feature that visibly uses aggregate data to help an individual customer.

**Brand reputation follows customers, not marketing.** With Jobber at 100,000+ customers and Housecall Pro at 2,700+, you are not competing on brand recognition yet. The practical move at this stage is to be findable in the places your buyer looks — trade association forums, HVAC and plumbing subreddits, the Capterra and G2 pages where your competitors are already reviewed — before you have enough reviews to rank. One real customer story from a named contractor in a specific trade is worth more here than a polished case study.

**Network effects and structural cost advantages are not this year's problem.** Field service software does not naturally produce network effects (one HVAC contractor's data does not make the product more valuable for another), and cost structure advantages require scale you have not reached. Do not invest in either dimension now — they are the most expensive moats to build from nothing and offer the least return at the seed stage. The right time to revisit them is when switching costs are moderate and you have a defined data story.

**No patent filings were found in the public record for Tessivane.** If you are describing the product as patent-protected in any investor materials, remove that language — there is no filing to point to. If you have filed and it has not yet published, that will show up in public records within 18 months of filing; until then, say "patent application pending" only if you have a filed application number you can provide on request.

---

### The outside review in plain terms

An outside review of this analysis ran and found three issues worth knowing. One is serious.

The serious finding is described above under investor questions: Tessivane's first-place rankings on both positioning maps rest on the startup's own description of itself, not on an independently measured score. An investor can ask a single question — "what external source puts you ahead of Jobber on simplicity?" — and the current answer is that the analysis positioned you there because you said you were simpler. Fix this with external evidence before using these maps in a pitch.

Two moderate findings round out the review: the exclusion of FieldPulse from the landscape (addressed above), and the absence of manual operations as a competitor category, which means neither map reflects the actual decision frame most of your target buyers are in — "should I keep using my whiteboard and phone, or should I buy something?" Including the status quo as a named alternative does not weaken your position; it shows you understand what you are actually selling against.

No outside review is a guarantee, and this one found real things worth fixing. The good news is that every finding points to a concrete action.

### What you have working in your favor

**Your carved-out position is real.** Across both maps — setup complexity and SMB-native design — no competitor lands ahead of you on both axes at the same time. ServiceTitan dominates platform breadth and scalability, but it is visibly heavier and more enterprise-oriented. Jobber and Housecall Pro are your nearest rivals, but the analysis puts clear space between you and each of them on the dimensions that matter most to your buyer. That is a defensible claim, not a platitude.

**The research on your three established competitors is thorough.** Pricing, funding, team size, and target customers were independently verified for ServiceTitan, Jobber, and Housecall Pro. The analysis does not dismiss their strengths — ServiceTitan's IPO scale, Jobber's 100,000+ customers, and Housecall Pro's AI acceleration are all acknowledged. That intellectual honesty is what makes your competitive framing credible in a diligence conversation.

**Your switching costs are building.** As customers accumulate job history, customer records, and operational workflows inside Tessivane, the cost of moving to another tool rises. That is the one defensibility dimension already in motion, and it is the right one to be building at this stage.

---

### The single highest-leverage fix before your next investor conversation

**Expand and diversify the competitive set.** The analysis covers three companies, all direct competitors. Investors expect to see at least five, and they expect to see more than one category — specifically a do-nothing alternative and at least one emerging entrant alongside the established direct rivals.

The candidates are already identified: FieldPulse (a direct SMB field service tool with nearly all of its reviewers from small businesses in exactly your target trades), the manual-operations alternative (phone calls, paper job cards, and shared spreadsheets — the actual incumbent for most sub-five-technician shops), and at least one of Workiz or Service Fusion as an emerging entrant. Adding these three does not change your position on the existing maps. What it does is show investors that you understand the full consideration set your buyer actually uses — and that you have a clear answer to why someone on spreadsheets would pay for Tessivane rather than continuing to do nothing.

Resolving this also fixes a related gap: right now, all three companies in your landscape are categorized identically, which signals narrow thinking to investors even when the research behind them is strong.

### How to prepare for the investor questions you will face

**Be ready for: "How do you know you're simpler than Jobber?"**

The analysis placed Tessivane first on both the setup-complexity map and the SMB-native design map. An outside review of this analysis raised a serious concern about both of those rankings: Tessivane's coordinates on each map were set by accepting your own positioning claim — that you are the lowest-complexity option — and then calibrating the number against Jobber and Housecall Pro. No external benchmark independently measures Tessivane's setup experience or SMB-nativeness today.

This is the question investors will ask, and the current answer is circular. Before your next meeting, gather evidence you didn't generate yourself: G2 or Capterra setup scores for Tessivane once you have enough reviews, onboarding completion rates from your paying customers, or a side-by-side setup time comparison run by an independent tester. Even a handful of customer quotes that specifically describe switching from Jobber and why the experience differed is stronger than a self-assigned score. The moment you have a non-self-referential data point, the first-place ranking becomes something you can defend in the room.

**Be ready for: "What's your edge over Jobber and Housecall Pro — aren't they already SMB-focused?"**

Your core differentiation claim — that Tessivane offers lighter-weight UX and pricing designed for smaller service businesses, not enterprise contractors — only partly holds under scrutiny. It is clearly true against ServiceTitan, where verifiable gaps in ease-of-setup scores support the comparison. It weakens significantly against Jobber and Housecall Pro, which already occupy the SMB-friendly field service software position with large installed customer bases.

You will need a sharper answer for this question than "we are simpler." One reframe worth building: Tessivane is built for the 2-to-10 technician shop that finds even Jobber's feature surface to be more than they need right now, and where the owner is still the one doing the scheduling. That is a narrower segment than Jobber addresses, but if it is yours, say so with numbers — how many shops in that range exist, what they currently pay, and why Jobber's pricing and onboarding does not fit them. A segmentation argument is more defensible than a simplicity argument when the incumbents are already in your category.

**Be ready for: "Who else is doing this?" (and know FieldPulse is on their list)**

FieldPulse was surfaced during this analysis's independent research. It targets HVAC, plumbing, and electrical SMBs — the same trades you name — with more than 450 reviews on Capterra, a 4.6 rating, and a direct positioning as field service management for small businesses. An investor who asks about your competitive set is likely to have seen it. Have a clear answer for why Tessivane and FieldPulse are not the same thing, whether that is a feature difference, a segment difference, or a geographic difference — but do not rely on the current analysis to answer that question, because FieldPulse does not appear in it.

### Defensibility roadmap: what to build, in what order

One defensibility dimension is in play today — switching costs — and it is early. Five others have not started yet. Here is how to think about the sequencing.

**Defend and deepen switching costs first.** This is already your strongest dimension (which is a low bar — it is currently weak), but it is also the cheapest to strengthen. The mechanism is workflow depth: the more of a customer's operational history lives inside Tessivane — past jobs, customer notes, recurring schedule patterns, invoice records — the harder it is to leave. Every feature that pulls more of the owner's real workflow into the product adds to this. Target: meaningful job-history depth and customer data portability that makes moving to Jobber feel like starting from scratch.

**Build data advantages in parallel.** As your customer base accumulates job data, you accumulate something competitors without your segment focus cannot easily replicate: a dataset of how 2-to-10-technician shops actually run — seasonal patterns, job type distributions, pricing norms for the trades verticals you serve. That data can improve your product (smarter scheduling suggestions, better invoice templates) and, eventually, become a reason buyers stay. This dimension is already moving in the right direction; the milestone to aim for is a product feature that visibly uses aggregate data to help an individual customer.

**Brand reputation follows customers, not marketing.** With Jobber at 100,000+ customers and Housecall Pro at 2,700+, you are not competing on brand recognition yet. The practical move at this stage is to be findable in the places your buyer looks — trade association forums, HVAC and plumbing subreddits, the Capterra and G2 pages where your competitors are already reviewed — before you have enough reviews to rank. One real customer story from a named contractor in a specific trade is worth more here than a polished case study.

**Network effects and structural cost advantages are not this year's problem.** Field service software does not naturally produce network effects (one HVAC contractor's data does not make the product more valuable for another), and cost structure advantages require scale you have not reached. Do not invest in either dimension now — they are the most expensive moats to build from nothing and offer the least return at the seed stage. The right time to revisit them is when switching costs are moderate and you have a defined data story.

**No patent filings were found in the public record for Tessivane.** If you are describing the product as patent-protected in any investor materials, remove that language — there is no filing to point to. If you have filed and it has not yet published, that will show up in public records within 18 months of filing; until then, say "patent application pending" only if you have a filed application number you can provide on request.

An outside review of this analysis ran and found three issues worth knowing. One is serious.

The serious finding is described above under investor questions: Tessivane's first-place rankings on both positioning maps rest on the startup's own description of itself, not on an independently measured score. Including the status quo as a named alternative does not weaken your position; it shows you understand what you are actually selling against.

No outside review is a guarantee, and this one found real things worth fixing. The good news is that every finding points to a concrete action.

## Differentiation Stress-Test

### SMB-first simplicity: lighter-weight UX and pricing designed for smaller service businesses, not enterprise contractors

- **Verdict:** Partially holds
- **Verifiable:** Yes
- **Evidence:** The claim is directionally verifiable on two dimensions. First, against ServiceTitan: independently researched evidence confirms ServiceTitan's onboarding is materially harder (G2 setup score 6.7 vs. 8.8–8.9 for SMB tools), and its pricing ($250–$398+/month) is out of reach for the smallest operators. Tessivane's positioning as lower-complexity and lower-cost is credible against that comparison. Second, against Jobber and Housecall Pro: both are already SMB-native (G2 setup scores 8.9 and 8.8 respectively, both under $300/month entry tiers), so the differentiating gap narrows significantly. Tessivane's claim holds clearly when the reference point is ServiceTitan but is harder to substantiate against the mid-tier SMB-focused incumbents.
- **Investor Challenge:** Investors will note that Jobber and Housecall Pro already occupy the 'SMB-friendly field service software' position and have done so for years with large customer bases (100K+ for Jobber). The claim 'not enterprise contractors' is accurate but not distinctive — Jobber and Housecall Pro also position against enterprise complexity. The question investors will ask is: what does Tessivane do that Jobber does not, at comparable or lower price? Without a sharper differentiator than 'simpler,' the claim partially holds but does not clearly separate Tessivane from two well-funded incumbents who occupy the same stated position.

## Coaching Commentary

### What you have working in your favor

**Your carved-out position is real.** Across both maps — setup complexity and SMB-native design — no competitor lands ahead of you on both axes at the same time. ServiceTitan dominates platform breadth and scalability, but it is visibly heavier and more enterprise-oriented. Jobber and Housecall Pro are your nearest rivals, but the analysis puts clear space between you and each of them on the dimensions that matter most to your buyer. That is a defensible claim, not a platitude.

**The research on your three established competitors is thorough.** Pricing, funding, team size, and target customers were independently verified for ServiceTitan, Jobber, and Housecall Pro. The analysis does not dismiss their strengths — ServiceTitan's IPO scale, Jobber's 100,000+ customers, and Housecall Pro's AI acceleration are all acknowledged. That intellectual honesty is what makes your competitive framing credible in a diligence conversation.

**Your switching costs are building.** As customers accumulate job history, customer records, and operational workflows inside Tessivane, the cost of moving to another tool rises. That is the one defensibility dimension already in motion, and it is the right one to be building at this stage.

---

### The single highest-leverage fix before your next investor conversation

**Expand and diversify the competitive set.** The analysis covers three companies, all direct competitors. Investors expect to see at least five, and they expect to see more than one category — specifically a do-nothing alternative and at least one emerging entrant alongside the established direct rivals.

The candidates are already identified: FieldPulse (a direct SMB field service tool with nearly all of its reviewers from small businesses in exactly your target trades), the manual-operations alternative (phone calls, paper job cards, and shared spreadsheets — the actual incumbent for most sub-five-technician shops), and at least one of Workiz or Service Fusion as an emerging entrant. Adding these three does not change your position on the existing maps. What it does is show investors that you understand the full consideration set your buyer actually uses — and that you have a clear answer to why someone on spreadsheets would pay for Tessivane rather than continuing to do nothing.

Resolving this also fixes a related gap: right now, all three companies in your landscape are categorized identically, which signals narrow thinking to investors even when the research behind them is strong.

---

### How to prepare for the investor questions you will face

**Be ready for: "How do you know you're simpler than Jobber?"**

The analysis placed Tessivane first on both the setup-complexity map and the SMB-native design map. An outside review of this analysis raised a serious concern about both of those rankings: Tessivane's coordinates on each map were set by accepting your own positioning claim — that you are the lowest-complexity option — and then calibrating the number against Jobber and Housecall Pro. No external benchmark independently measures Tessivane's setup experience or SMB-nativeness today.

This is the question investors will ask, and the current answer is circular. Before your next meeting, gather evidence you didn't generate yourself: G2 or Capterra setup scores for Tessivane once you have enough reviews, onboarding completion rates from your paying customers, or a side-by-side setup time comparison run by an independent tester. Even a handful of customer quotes that specifically describe switching from Jobber and why the experience differed is stronger than a self-assigned score. The moment you have a non-self-referential data point, the first-place ranking becomes something you can defend in the room.

**Be ready for: "What's your edge over Jobber and Housecall Pro — aren't they already SMB-focused?"**

Your core differentiation claim — that Tessivane offers lighter-weight UX and pricing designed for smaller service businesses, not enterprise contractors — only partly holds under scrutiny. It is clearly true against ServiceTitan, where verifiable gaps in ease-of-setup scores support the comparison. It weakens significantly against Jobber and Housecall Pro, which already occupy the SMB-friendly field service software position with large installed customer bases.

You will need a sharper answer for this question than "we are simpler." One reframe worth building: Tessivane is built for the 2-to-10 technician shop that finds even Jobber's feature surface to be more than they need right now, and where the owner is still the one doing the scheduling. That is a narrower segment than Jobber addresses, but if it is yours, say so with numbers — how many shops in that range exist, what they currently pay, and why Jobber's pricing and onboarding does not fit them. A segmentation argument is more defensible than a simplicity argument when the incumbents are already in your category.

**Be ready for: "Who else is doing this?" (and know FieldPulse is on their list)**

FieldPulse was surfaced during this analysis's independent research. It targets HVAC, plumbing, and electrical SMBs — the same trades you name — with more than 450 reviews on Capterra, a 4.6 rating, and a direct positioning as field service management for small businesses. An investor who asks about your competitive set is likely to have seen it. Have a clear answer for why Tessivane and FieldPulse are not the same thing, whether that is a feature difference, a segment difference, or a geographic difference — but do not rely on the current analysis to answer that question, because FieldPulse does not appear in it.

---

### Defensibility roadmap: what to build, in what order

One defensibility dimension is in play today — switching costs — and it is early. Five others have not started yet. Here is how to think about the sequencing.

**Defend and deepen switching costs first.** This is already your strongest dimension (which is a low bar — it is currently weak), but it is also the cheapest to strengthen. The mechanism is workflow depth: the more of a customer's operational history lives inside Tessivane — past jobs, customer notes, recurring schedule patterns, invoice records — the harder it is to leave. Every feature that pulls more of the owner's real workflow into the product adds to this. Target: meaningful job-history depth and customer data portability that makes moving to Jobber feel like starting from scratch.

**Build data advantages in parallel.** As your customer base accumulates job data, you accumulate something competitors without your segment focus cannot easily replicate: a dataset of how 2-to-10-technician shops actually run — seasonal patterns, job type distributions, pricing norms for the trades verticals you serve. That data can improve your product (smarter scheduling suggestions, better invoice templates) and, eventually, become a reason buyers stay. This dimension is already moving in the right direction; the milestone to aim for is a product feature that visibly uses aggregate data to help an individual customer.

**Brand reputation follows customers, not marketing.** With Jobber at 100,000+ customers and Housecall Pro at 2,700+, you are not competing on brand recognition yet. The practical move at this stage is to be findable in the places your buyer looks — trade association forums, HVAC and plumbing subreddits, the Capterra and G2 pages where your competitors are already reviewed — before you have enough reviews to rank. One real customer story from a named contractor in a specific trade is worth more here than a polished case study.

**Network effects and structural cost advantages are not this year's problem.** Field service software does not naturally produce network effects (one HVAC contractor's data does not make the product more valuable for another), and cost structure advantages require scale you have not reached. Do not invest in either dimension now — they are the most expensive moats to build from nothing and offer the least return at the seed stage. The right time to revisit them is when switching costs are moderate and you have a defined data story.

**No patent filings were found in the public record for Tessivane.** If you are describing the product as patent-protected in any investor materials, remove that language — there is no filing to point to. If you have filed and it has not yet published, that will show up in public records within 18 months of filing; until then, say "patent application pending" only if you have a filed application number you can provide on request.

---

### The outside review in plain terms

An outside review of this analysis ran and found three issues worth knowing. One is serious.

The serious finding is described above under investor questions: Tessivane's first-place rankings on both positioning maps rest on the startup's own description of itself, not on an independently measured score. An investor can ask a single question — "what external source puts you ahead of Jobber on simplicity?" — and the current answer is that the analysis positioned you there because you said you were simpler. Fix this with external evidence before using these maps in a pitch.

Two moderate findings round out the review: the exclusion of FieldPulse from the landscape (addressed above), and the absence of manual operations as a competitor category, which means neither map reflects the actual decision frame most of your target buyers are in — "should I keep using my whiteboard and phone, or should I buy something?" Including the status quo as a named alternative does not weaken your position; it shows you understand what you are actually selling against.

No outside review is a guarantee, and this one found real things worth fixing. The good news is that every finding points to a concrete action.
